employer support services and GOV.UK guidance:

The Home Office Employer Enquiry helpline on 0300 790 6268

Penalties for employing illegal workers which provides access to guidance on preventing illegal working

Reporting suspected illegal working

Where an employer wishes to report suspected illegal working within their workforce, they should be directed to the appropriate employer reporting route as set out in the code of practice and current employer guidance.

An employer who reports suspected illegal working and obtains a Unique Reference Number (URN) before the Home Office identifies the individual may qualify for a reduction in any subsequent civil penalty in respect of that illegal worker. The Civil Penalty Compliance Team (CPCT) will determine whether the relevant mitigating criteria are met.

Requests concerning an individual’s right to work

Where an employer requires help with the process of conducting a right to work check, direct them to the current published guidance and employer support services.

You must not advise an employer to dismiss an individual, terminate a working arrangement, or make any other employment decision. Employers remain responsible for carrying out the prescribed checks and deciding what action to take in relation to their workers.

Compliance and educational visits to employers

Advice and instruction visits (‘compliance visits’ or ‘educational visits’) may be undertaken to help employers and other persons within scope of the Right to Work Scheme to understand their responsibilities and how to prevent illegal working.

Where relevant, a compliance or educational visit may cover:

responsibilities under the Right to Work Scheme

how to carry out prescribed right to work checks

the requirements for establishing a statutory excuse, including where the extended liability provisions apply

relevant GOV.UK guidance and online services

where to obtain further information and support

the limits of the advice that Home Office officials can provide

You must not use a compliance or an educational visit to determine liability in advance, advise on individual employment decisions, or give assurances that civil penalty or criminal action will not follow.

Compliance or educational visits must be tasked, authorised and risk assessed in accordance with current operational requirements and carried out by suitably trained officers. They do not provide any additional powers of entry, search, questioning, or seizure.

Consent

Compliance or educational visits must be conducted with the informed consent of the employer or another individual responsible for the business who has authority to give consent. The employer or other responsible person should complete the Consent for compliance visit form before the visit and consent should be confirmed on arrival.

The individual who gave consent may withdraw it at any time. If consent is withdrawn before entry, the visit must not proceed. If it is withdrawn during the visit, officers must leave the premises.

The scope of the visit must remain consistent with that agreed with the individual who gave consent.

For all standard enforcement visits, the employer or another individual responsible for the business is served with a Notice to occupier form on entry.

Suspected illegal working during a compliance or educational visit

If you identify suspected illegal working during a compliance or educational visit, you must record the relevant information and evidence on Pronto, or the current approved operational system, and make the appropriate intelligence referral.

Where the circumstances indicate potential criminality, a safeguarding concern, or an immediate operational risk, stop the compliance or educational activity and follow the relevant operational guidance.

Version 2.0

Access, Compliance, Removals and Enforcement General Instructions

About this guidance

This guidance provides information for Immigration Enforcement officers (“you”) on how to conduct an illegal working operation. It does not replace the legislation, civil penalty regulations, or code of practice, and should be read together with relevant sections and articles mentioned within.

Contacts

If you have read the relevant legislation, this guide and the Employer’s guide to right to work checks and still require more help with an illegal working operation, you must ask your line manager for assistance in the first instance.

If the question cannot be answered at line manager level, you may email (as appropriate):

Civil Penalty Compliance Team (CPCT) communication and correspondence

Right to Work Policy Team

Criminal and Financial Investigations

Enforcement Policy

The Work Casework Risk Team

You can signpost employers who have general enquiries about illegal working and right to work checks to the Home Office Employer Enquiry helpline on 0300 790 6268.

If you notice any formatting errors in this guidance (broken links, spelling mistakes and so on) or have any comments about the layout or navigability of the guidance then you can contact the Guidance Rules and Forms Team.

The full list of documents and tools that support employers are:

Employer’s guide to right to work checks

Right to Work Checklist

Code of practice on preventing illegal working: Right to Work Scheme for employers

Avoiding discrimination while preventing illegal working: code of practice

Illegal working civil penalties: an employer’s guide

an online interactive tool Checking a job applicant’s right to work

an online interactive tool Employer Checking Service

Publication

Below is information on when this version of the guidance was published:

version 2.0

published for Home Office staff on 26 October 2026

Changes from the last version of this guidance

updated guidance to reflect changes introduced by Section 48 of the Border Security, Asylum and Immigration Act 2025, including the extension of the Right to Work Scheme (“the Scheme”) and associated civil penalty liability from 1 October 2026 to a wider range of working arrangements - this includes individuals engaged under a worker’s contract, individual sub-contractors, and certain online matching services

updated definitions throughout the guidance, including the definitions of ‘illegal worker’, ‘working illegally’, and organisations or persons who may be liable for a civil penalty under the Scheme, to align with current legislation and policy

updated references to the latest Employer’s guide to right to work checks and Code of Practice on preventing illegal working

updated criminal offence and civil penalty references to reflect current legislation, including the offence of knowingly employing, or having reasonable cause to believe, that an individual is disqualified from working

updated sponsorship guidance to reflect current sponsor compliance processes and referral arrangements

removed superseded material, including guidance on Croatian national employment restrictions, and consolidated related material on evidence gathering, criminal action, statutory excuses, and supporting employers.

reviewed and updated contact details, cross-references and links to related guidance, legislation, and operational products

general updates to terminology, formatting and drafting to improve consistency with current Home Office guidance standards, including replacing references to ’employees’ with ’workers’, where appropriate

Legislation

You must be familiar with the following legislation when conducting illegal working operations:

Sections 14A to 25 – Immigration, Asylum and Nationality Act 2006

The Immigration (Restrictions on Employment) Order 2007

Section 24B - Immigration Act 1971

The legislation listed above provides the core legal framework for the prevention of illegal working in the UK, including right to work checks, the working arrangements within scope of the Scheme, and the civil and criminal sanctions that may apply.

Legislation What it covers

Sections 14A to 25 of the Immigration, Asylum and Nationality Act 2006. The Right to Work Scheme, including civil penalty liability under the Scheme and the criminal offence relating to employing an individual who is disqualified from working by reason of their immigration status.

The Immigration (Restrictions on Employment) Order 2007. The requirements relating to right to work checks and establishing a statutory excuse against civil penalty liability.

Section 24B of the Immigration Act 1971. The criminal offence of illegal working.

When the Right to Work Scheme applies

The Scheme has applied to employment (under a contract of service or apprenticeship) commencing on or after 29 February 2008.

From 1 October 2026, the scheme also applies to a wider range of working arrangements, including where an organisation either:

engages an individual under a worker’s contract

engages an individual sub-contractor

operates an online matching service that provides details of individual service providers to potential clients or customers

In some circumstances, civil penalty liability may also extend beyond the employer who has the direct contractual relationship with the worker. Further guidance on extended liability is provided below.

The changes introduced from 1 October 2026 are not retrospective. This means they do not create liability under new provisions in relation to working arrangements entered into before that date.

You must consider the potential nature of the working arrangement to guide your questioning and gather evidence about how it operates and when it commenced. The Civil Penalty Compliance Team (CPCT) will consider the evidence and determine the type of working arrangement and the provisions that apply.

Additional evidence

Information obtained through questioning should be considered alongside any other relevant evidence identified during the operation.

Observations

Your observations may help to establish how the working arrangement operates in practice and corroborate or clarify information provided by the worker, employer, or person in charge.

Documentary, photographic, and digital evidence

Documents, photographs, and digital material may also provide evidence about the working arrangement. You must ensure that you have the appropriate lawful authority to obtain or record such evidence. See: Search and seizure.

Extended liability

In certain contractual arrangements, civil penalty liability may extend beyond the employer who has the direct contractual relationship with the worker. This is known as extended liability. Extended liability may apply where either:

a person is contracted to provide work or services to a third party and contracts with another employer who employs workers to carry out all or part of the work or services required to fulfil that contract

an online matching service matches a service provider with a client or customer to provide work or services, and the service provider enters into a contract with the client or customer

an employer employs an individual to provide work or services, and the contract permits that individual to substitute their work or services to be carried out by another individual in their place

The starting point is to identify the employer who has the direct contractual relationship with the worker. That employer remains responsible for carrying out the prescribed right to work check and establishing a statutory excuse. Extended liability does not automatically transfer that responsibility to another person in the contractual arrangement.

Where the direct employer cannot be identified, liability may, in the relevant circumstances described, extend to another organisation in the contractual arrangements.

Gathering information about extended liability

You are not required to determine whether extended liability applies. You should gather sufficient information and evidence to enable CPCT to assess the contractual arrangements and determine liability.

Issuing notices

This section explains when and how to issue a no action notice (NAN-E) or a Notice of Potential Liability (NOPL) where illegal working is identified.

An employer may establish a statutory excuse against liability for a civil penalty by either:

carrying out the prescribed right to work check before the worker commences employment, and where required, carrying out any follow-up checks for workers with a time-limited right to work (as shown by an expiry date)

where the extended liability provisions apply, complying with the prescribed requirements relating to the relevant contractual arrangements

Issuing a no action notice (NAN-E)

Considering evidence of a statutory excuse

Where you identify an illegal worker during an operation, you must give the employer or an appropriate person representing the employer or the business an opportunity to provide evidence that a statutory excuse has been established.

You must consider any evidence provided in support of a statutory excuse in accordance with the Code of Practice on preventing illegal working and the published Employer’s guide to right to work checks.

The officer in charge (OIC) must decide on the basis of the evidence available during the operation, whether to issue a NAN-E or a Notice of Potential Liability (NOPL). Where there is clear evidence that a statutory excuse has been established, a NAN-E must be issued. Where there is no clear evidence of a statutory excuse, a NOPL must be issued and the case referred to the Civil Penalty Compliance Team (CPCT).

A NAN-E must be issued at the time of the visit to the employer or a representative of the business in respect of each illegal worker for whom there is clear evidence that a statutory excuse has been established.

Issuing a Notice of Potential Liability (NOPL)

Where illegal working is identified and there is no clear evidence during the operation that a statutory excuse has been established, you must issue a NOPL to the employer or an appropriate representative of the business.

Potential extended liability

Where potential extended liability is identified during a visit, you must issue a NOPL to each potentially liable employer or person present at the premises. This may require more than 1 NOPL to be issued.
